thesis.line: So far the picks circle one question: how strangers form communities they can leave, live in, choose between, and keep alive.
thesis.paragraph:
Since October 2026, the people who now run Farcaster have been paying the network to learn in public: build a client, explain an idea in 59 seconds, and get paid in USDC. Each prize is a different subject. Read side by side, they connect, sometimes directly and sometimes only abstractly.

This atlas collects the answers, puts the best first, adds the sources and the strongest objections, and draws the connections. It updates itself as new prizes and new answers arrive. This note is the editor's current reading of the through-line, and it will be revised as the picks accumulate.

archetype.name: The Founder-Citizen
archetype.line: Someone who can found a community that lasts, and be a good member of one. Each strand you read deepens one side of them.

strands.name: Tools you own
strands.line: The protocols, keys and nodes that make leaving and building possible.

facet.name: Sovereign
facet.grant: You can leave with your name, your graph and your words.

strands.name: Norms & trust
strands.line: How strangers come to cooperate: manners, codes, reputation and enforcement.

facet.name: Civil
facet.grant: You can disagree with a stranger without making an enemy.

strands.name: Exit & choice
strands.line: Many communities, mobile people, and what competition between them does.

facet.name: Mobile
facet.grant: You choose your communities on purpose, and you let others choose theirs.

strands.name: Founding & endurance
strands.line: How communities start, govern themselves, and survive their founders.

facet.name: Enduring
facet.grant: You know why communities die, and what the ones that lasted had in common.

prizes.headline: Hello everyone! Network School is acquiring Farcaster.
prizes.gloss: Announces the acquisition and a four-step plan: enforce moderation rules, run an onchain vote, publish a social smart contract and Network Code with examples of good and bad behavior, and host meetups. Other clients remain permitted but may not use the Farcaster or Network School names for tokens or commercial projects.

prizes.headline: $2048 FOR FARCASTER CLIENTS
prizes.deliverable: A microsite (quickstart + tutorial), an MIT-licensed repo, and a public vouch from a human who completed it: provision compute, run a Snapchain read node, and run a client that reads from it — three commands, no API keys.

prizes.headline: $2048 IN PRIZES FOR VIDEOS ON NORBERT ELIAS & CIVILITY
prizes.deliverable: A vertical 9:16 video of about 59 seconds explaining Norbert Elias's account of how manners and peer-to-peer self-restraint rebuilt large-scale cooperation — concrete enough for a viewer with no context, linking civility to wealth and physical safety.

context.headline: THE RESTORATION OF FRIEND SPEECH ($2048 PRIZE)
context.gloss: After an onchain vote (26,000+ votes, ~95% for a moderated reference client; ~271 accounts moderated; ~4% opted out), argues civility — as in high-trust Singapore — enables large-scale cooperation and a stronger digital economy.

prizes.headline: $1024 IN PRIZES FOR VIDEOS ON THE COMMUNISTIC SOCIETIES OF THE UNITED STATES
prizes.deliverable: A vertical 9:16 video, 59 seconds or less, for a viewer with no context: what Nordhoff's communities had in common, why some lasted a century while others collapsed within years, and what new communities can learn. AI tools allowed; AI slop is not.
references: Charles Nordhoff, The Communistic Societies of the United States (1875) — free on Project Gutenberg, shared by @farcaster in 0x117d527b2fad88814c97df3cd38ed56b59bb78ff

prizes.headline: $1000 FOR NETWORK STATE VISUALS
prizes.deliverable: Fully open-source visuals of how a network state forms, submitted as replies with the tools used and links to the raw files.

submissions.gloss: Civility as social technology: how strangers share space without a ruler's monopoly on violence.
Manners as an early trust protocol for high-trust economies.
Civility builds the trust that makes cooperation and business possible.
Singapore's measured trust is modest; what's world-class is predictability. Is the lever politeness or enforcement?
A journalist's 1870s tour of 72 communes, and what discipline had to do with survival.
How big these communities were, through an 1874 visitor's eyes.
